title: Set Work Study: Esperanza Spalding – Samba Em Preludio
content_html:
Context: From Bossa Nova Classic to Jazz Reinvention

Esperanza Spalding is an American jazz bassist, vocalist and composer known for combining virtuosic acoustic bass guitar playing with a warm, agile singing voice. On her album ‘Esperanza’, she recorded a version of ‘Samba Em Preludio’, a song originally written in 1962 by the Brazilian guitarist Baden Powell and the poet and lyricist Vinicius de Moraes. This original pairing was central to the bossa nova movement, a gentle, jazz-influenced offshoot of Brazilian samba that swept through popular music in the early 1960s.

Spalding’s recording is a fusion set work because it takes a song rooted in Brazilian popular tradition and filters it through the harmonic language, instrumentation and improvisatory freedom of jazz. The Portuguese-language vocal line is preserved, keeping the piece anchored in its Brazilian identity, while the surrounding arrangement — acoustic bass guitar, acoustic guitar and strings — reshapes the song’s sound world for a contemporary jazz audience.

Bossa nova blends samba rhythms with cool jazz harmony and understated, intimate vocal delivery, favouring subtlety over the louder, more percussive energy of traditional samba.

The Original Song and Its Transformation

In its original form, ‘Samba em Prelúdio’ is a samba-canção, a slow, reflective ballad style, built around Baden Powell’s intricate fingerstyle guitar accompaniment. The song’s minor-key melancholy and gently syncopated guitar patterns became a defining sound of the bossa nova era, valued for its harmonic sophistication and understated emotional intensity.

Listening to the source material helps you understand what Spalding keeps and what she changes. The embed below is a recording rooted in the song’s original guitar-and-voice tradition. As you listen, notice the soft dynamic level throughout, the delicate syncopation in the guitar part (chords placed fractionally off the beat), and the way the melody unfolds slowly over sustained, close-position harmony rather than driving rhythmic energy.

Spalding keeps this reflective mood but reimagines the texture: instead of solo guitar carrying both melody and harmony, she opens with just voice and acoustic bass guitar, later building outward into a fuller jazz ensemble sound that includes guitar and strings.

Opening Texture: The Duet of Voice and Double Bass

The recording begins with the acoustic bass guitar alone; the voice joins moments later in a stripped-back rubato duet. This intimate opening immediately signals the fusion of jazz and Brazilian song, since the acoustic bass guitar — more associated with jazz combos than traditional bossa nova groups — takes on a melodic, almost conversational role rather than simply outlining the harmony from below.

The bass line moves between supporting pizzicato notes that outline the chord roots and more active, melodically shaped phrases that interact with the vocal line, creating a sense of dialogue between the two parts. This is a texture technique worth naming precisely in your listening exam: it is best described as a duet, or two-part texture, rather than simply ‘thin’ or ‘quiet’.

A duet texture between voice and acoustic bass guitar allows Spalding to showcase both her vocal lyricism and her instrumental fluency, reinforcing her identity as a bassist-vocalist within a single opening gesture.

Building the Texture: Guitar, Comping and Strings

As the arrangement develops, an acoustic guitar enters, providing bossa nova-style comping: light, syncopated chordal patterns that echo the harmonic rhythm of the original Baden Powell accompaniment while sitting underneath the bass and voice rather than dominating them. This use of comping keeps a clear link to the song’s Brazilian roots even as the overall sound becomes more layered and jazz-inflected.

Later in the track, a guitar-led texture is introduced, adding sustained, lush harmonic colour behind the voice, bass and guitar. The strings thicken the texture from a lean, intimate opening into a fuller, more orchestral sound, while still allowing the voice and bass to remain the primary melodic focus. This gradual layering — duet, then guitar, then strings — is a clear example of texture building through addition of instrumental layers, a feature examiners frequently ask students to trace across a set work extract.

Use the embed below to follow this layering in real time. Listen for the exact moment the guitar joins the bass and voice, and then for the point where the strings enter, noticing how the dynamic level and harmonic richness both increase as each new layer is added.

Notice too how Spalding’s vocal delivery stays soft and unforced even as the ensemble around her grows fuller — this restraint is typical of both bossa nova performance style and Spalding’s own jazz aesthetic.

Tonality, Harmony and Melodic Lyricism

The piece is set in a minor key, which supports the song’s reflective, bittersweet character. Bossa nova harmony typically favours extended and altered chords — sevenths, ninths and occasionally more complex jazz voicings — layered smoothly beneath a lyrical, stepwise melodic line, and Spalding’s arrangement preserves this harmonic sophistication rather than simplifying it for a pop context.

The melody itself moves in long, flowing phrases, often using gentle rubato (small, expressive flexibility of tempo) rather than a strict, metronomic pulse. This rubato phrasing, combined with the minor tonality and rich harmony, creates the intimate, unhurried lyricism that is central to both the bossa nova tradition and Spalding’s personal jazz style.

Minor-key tonality combined with extended jazz harmony and rubato phrasing produces the reflective, lyrical mood that links this fusion recording back to its 1962 bossa nova origins.

Applying This to Your Listening Exam

When answering questions on this set work, always be precise about texture: name the specific layers present (voice, acoustic bass guitar, guitar, strings) rather than using vague terms like ‘full’ or ‘thin’. Similarly, when discussing tonality or harmony, refer to the minor key and the use of extended jazz chords rather than simply saying the harmony is ‘interesting’ or ‘complex’.

Also be ready to explain how this recording fits the definition of a fusion: it combines a genre rooted in Brazilian popular song (bossa nova/samba) with the instrumentation, harmonic language and improvisatory sensibility of jazz, and it foregrounds a performer — Spalding — whose own musical identity spans both traditions.
exam_tip_html: If asked to describe how texture changes across an extract, do not just list the instruments — describe the order and effect of their entries, for example: ‘the texture begins as a duet between voice and acoustic bass guitar, then thickens as acoustic guitar comping is added, before becoming fuller still with the entry of sustained string chords, increasing the overall dynamic and harmonic richness’. A common mistake is naming instruments correctly but never explaining the effect of their layering on texture and mood, which loses marks even when the identification is accurate.
conclusion_html: Samba Em Preludio shows how a jazz musician can honour the mood and harmonic language of a 1962 bossa nova classic while reshaping its texture and instrumentation into something distinctly her own. Revise the layering of voice, acoustic bass guitar and acoustic guitar, the minor-key lyricism, and the link back to Baden Powell and Vinicius de Moraes, then test yourself with the practice questions below.

practice_questions.text: Identify the two instruments that open Spalding's recording of Samba Em Preludio.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark for correctly naming voice and acoustic bass guitar.

practice_questions.text: Name the original songwriters credited with writing Samba em Prelúdio in 1962.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark for naming Baden Powell and Vinicius de Moraes.

practice_questions.text: Describe how the texture develops across the recording from the opening to the entry of the strings.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for identifying the duet opening, the addition of guitar comping, and the later entry of strings, with credit for describing the resulting increase in fullness.

practice_questions.text: Explain how this recording can be described as a fusion of styles.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for reference to combining Brazilian bossa nova/samba song tradition with jazz instrumentation, harmony and performance style, referencing Spalding's dual identity as bassist and vocalist.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effect of the minor tonality and rubato phrasing on the character of the piece.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for linking minor key and flexible tempo to the reflective, lyrical, bittersweet mood of the song.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how Spalding's arrangement both preserves and transforms features of the original bossa nova song.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for balanced discussion covering preserved features (Portuguese lyric, minor key, bossa nova harmony/comping) and transformed features (opening duet texture, added strings, jazz-influenced instrumentation), with clear supporting detail.

knowledge_checks.q: Who originally wrote Samba em Prelúdio in 1962?
options: Antonio Carlos Jobim and João Gilberto
Baden Powell and Vinicius de Moraes

knowledge_checks.q: What texture opens Spalding's recording of Samba Em Preludio?
options: A duet between voice and acoustic bass guitar

knowledge_checks.q: What role does the acoustic guitar play when it enters the arrangement?
options: It plays a fast improvised solo
It provides bossa nova-style syncopated comping
It doubles the bass line exactly
It plays a strict march rhythm

knowledge_checks.q: What is the overall tonality of the piece?
options: Modal with no clear key centre

knowledge_checks.q: Which genre is bossa nova generally considered to be a blend of?
options: Samba rhythms and cool jazz harmony

glossary_terms.definition: A gentle Brazilian style blending samba rhythms with cool jazz harmony, popularised in the early 1960s.
A slow, reflective Brazilian ballad style that preceded and influenced bossa nova.
Music that combines elements from two or more distinct genres or traditions.
A musical texture created by exactly two performing parts sounding together.
Short for accompanying; playing chordal rhythmic patterns to support a melody, common in jazz and bossa nova guitar or piano parts.
An acoustic-bodied bass guitar whose four strings provide the lowest pitched line in this recording.
Expressive flexibility of tempo, slightly speeding up or slowing down for musical effect.
A tonality built on a minor scale, often associated with a darker or more reflective mood.
Rhythmic accents placed off the main beats, creating a sense of rhythmic surprise or groove.
A playing technique where string instrument notes are plucked rather than bowed.
The gradual addition of instrumental parts to build a fuller, richer texture over time.

description: This lesson explores how Esperanza Spalding reworks a 1962 Brazilian bossa nova classic into an intimate jazz fusion built around voice, acoustic bass guitar and acoustic guitar.
